answers.solution:
The off-by-one error is in the loop condition of the tick counting function. Using `i <= n` causes the function to read **n+1** ticks instead of **n** ticks. This is most clearly visible when `n=179`: the buggy version reads 180 ticks.

### Buggy code (`ticker.go` - `CountTicks`):

```go
func CountTicks(c <-chan time.Time, n int) int {
    count := 0
    for i := 0; i <= n; i++ {  // BUG: <= causes n+1 iterations
        <-c
        count++
    }
    return count
}
```

### Fixed code (`ticker.go` - `WaitForTicks`):

```go
func WaitForTicks(c <-chan time.Time, n int) int {
    count := 0
    for i := 0; i < n; i++ {   // FIX: < gives exactly n iterations
        <-c
        count++
    }
    return count
}
```

The fix changes `<=` to `<` in the loop condition, reducing the iteration count by 1. For `n=179`, the buggy version loops `0,1,2,...,179` (180 iterations), while the fixed version loops `0,1,2,...,178` (179 iterations).

---

All tests pass confirming both the bug and the fix:

```

    ticker_test.go:19: BUG CONFIRMED: CountTicks(5) reads 6 ticks (off by one: <= reads one extra)

--- PASS: TestCountTicks179/fixed_version_reads_exactly_179

=== RUN   TestWaitForTicksEdgeCases
=== RUN   TestWaitForTicksEdgeCases/zero_ticks     --- PASS
=== RUN   TestWaitForTicksEdgeCases/one_tick       --- PASS

PASS
ok  	tickproblem	0.407s
```

**Edge cases tested:**
| Case | Buggy (`<=`) | Fixed (`<`) |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| n=0 | reads 1 tick (wrong) | reads 0 ticks (correct) |
| n=1 | reads 2 ticks (wrong) | reads 1 tick (correct) |
| n=5 | reads 6 ticks (wrong) | reads 5 ticks (correct) |
| n=100 | reads 101 ticks (wrong) | reads 100 ticks (correct) |
| **n=179** | **reads 180 ticks (wrong)** | **reads 179 ticks (correct)** |
